title: Adversarial Robustness in Diffusion Policy Systems via Latent Space Perturbation Analysis
summary: This work investigates adversarial vulnerabilities in diffusion-based policy systems by analyzing latent space perturbations. We propose a novel attack framework that identifies critical timesteps and spatial regions in diffusion processes where minimal perturbations cause maximal policy failure. The approach combines gradient-based optimization with physical constraint modeling to generate both digital and physical adversarial examples. Validation involves measuring success rate degradation across manipulation tasks under various attack scenarios.
gap: Current diffusion policy safety research focuses on end-to-end attacks without analyzing how vulnerabilities manifest across diffusion timesteps or spatial dimensions.
approach: We develop a multi-stage attack methodology: (1) timestep sensitivity analysis to identify critical diffusion phases, (2) spatial saliency mapping to locate vulnerable regions, and (3) constrained optimization to generate minimal perturbations. The framework includes both white-box and black-box attack variants, with physical realizability constraints for tangible adversarial objects.
evaluation: We test against pre-trained diffusion policies on manipulation benchmarks, measuring success rate drops under digital/physical attacks. Comparisons include baseline methods like DP-Attacker and random perturbation baselines. Additional metrics assess transferability across policy architectures and perturbation detectability.
